Animated sprites select successive source images over time, often from a [[Sprite Sheet]]. Sprites remain the primary visual building block of many 2D games even though modern displays and assets are much larger than their early counterparts.

A spurious correlation is a statistical association that does not reflect the causal relationship a decision maker assumes. Variables may move together by chance, because both depend on another factor, or because the data collection process created the pattern.

Machine learning can exploit such associations successfully within training data while failing when conditions change. The ethical risk grows when correlation is used to judge a person, allocate an opportunity, or justify intervention. High predictive performance does not by itself establish that the inferred relationship is meaningful, fair, or appropriate for action.

A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns, so its size is $n\times n$. Square shape permits operations and properties that rectangular matrices do not have, including a [[Determinant]], [[Matrix Trace]], eigenvalues, and possibly a [[Matrix Inverse]].

A square matrix is strictly diagonally dominant when, in every row, the absolute diagonal entry is greater than the sum of the absolute values of all other entries in that row.

This structural condition guarantees nonsingularity and supplies a useful sufficient condition for convergence of the [[Jacobi Method]] and [[Gauss-Seidel Method]]. It is sufficient, not necessary: some nondominant systems also converge.

A stabilized approach keeps configuration, speed, power, vertical path, sink rate, and checklists within the aircraft and operator's defined limits by a specified altitude. Those conditions must then remain stable through landing. If they are not achieved or are lost, a go-around is the planned corrective action rather than an exceptional failure.

A stacked area time-series plot accumulates component series so the outer boundary represents their total. It is meaningful when the variables are additive parts of a global quantity and supports reading contribution and total change together. Only the first component has a stable baseline; internal layers are harder to compare precisely. Layer order therefore affects interpretation, and components that do not form a meaningful sum should not be stacked.

A stacked autoencoder builds a deep representation by placing several encoders in sequence. Layers may be pretrained one at a time as autoencoders before the entire stack is fine-tuned.

Successive hidden layers transform the input into increasingly abstract features. Bottlenecks, sparsity, denoising, and supervised objectives can be combined to shape the learned representation.

A stacked bar chart partitions each bar according to the levels of a second categorical variable. It shows both the size of the primary groups and how the secondary outcome is distributed within them.

The first segment has a common baseline, while later segments do not, so subtle comparisons can be difficult. Frequencies, proportions, and the intended denominator should therefore be made explicit in the labels or accompanying table.

The book uses the stacked form to display a second category within each group and contrasts it with filled and dodged variants. That comparison makes the choice of denominator and baseline an explicit design decision.

A stage gate is a deliberate checkpoint at which a project is evaluated for viability, progress, risk, and continued investment. A concept may pass forward, return for significant revision, or be removed from active development.

Stage gates bound an otherwise open-ended [[Design-Build-Test Loop]]. They allow exploration while preventing iteration from becoming indefinite motion without progress, and they preserve rejected ideas for possible future use rather than forcing sunk-cost continuation.

A gate can coexist with agile delivery when it evaluates demonstrated results, current risks, and updated forecasts. Treating the gate as approval of a frozen speculative plan instead suppresses the evidence that iteration was meant to produce.

A staging deployment installs a release candidate into a nonproduction environment before live promotion. It provides a hosted destination for checking the artifact, environment settings, network relationships, and application startup.

Passing staging supplies additional release evidence but does not erase environmental differences. The pipeline must use the correct staging configuration and define how promotion follows verification.

A staging environment is a pre-production deployment used to verify a published application under conditions closer to production than ordinary development. It creates a place to test configuration, hosting, networking, and deployment output before public release.

Staging should remain separate from production data and credentials while resembling the production topology closely enough to expose environment-specific faults.

A staging slot is a nonproduction App Service destination used to host a release candidate before promotion. The deployment pipeline can install the new artifact there and run checks against an accessible environment.

Staging provides evidence about the deployable package and hosted configuration without immediately replacing production. It is useful only when its differences from production are understood and intentional.

A stakeholder is a person or group with a meaningful interest in a product's outcome. Players, publishers, platform holders, business leaders, and dependent teams can each supply constraints, feedback, or value judgments.

Stakeholders collaborate through the [[Product Owner]] and inspect working results at the [[Sprint Review]]. Their participation grounds decisions in product evidence without turning the Development Team into a committee-controlled task pool.

A standard error is the standard deviation of a statistic's [[Sampling Distribution]]. It measures how much the estimate would vary if the data-generating and sampling process were repeated.

For a sample mean under the [[Central Limit Theorem]], the population standard deviation is divided by the square root of sample size. In practice the unknown population spread is estimated, which introduces the t-distribution in small samples.

For example, if you decide to notify development teams about new deployments in their Slack, you

To sum it up, using a well-defined set of life cycle events across all tools and phases enables many

• Traceability: We can trace every artifact from its initial creation until its end of the life cycle.

responsible for letting an artifact into a certain environment.
• Measurement: We can measure how many artifacts flow through the life cycle and how long
it takes. This is the basis for reporting the DORA Efficiency metrics!
• Interoperability: We can easily integrate new tools or replace them if they all adhere to the
same standards (e.g., switching from one notification tool to another is just a matter of changing
an event subscription).
• Flexibility: Like replacing tools, we can easily adapt our delivery processes by having additional
tools add work on certain events (e.g., adding an additional mandatory security scan for
deployments in certain environments can be done by an event subscription of a security scan tool).

A standing wave forms when similar waves traveling in opposite directions superpose. Fixed nodes have zero amplitude, while antinodes have maximum amplitude, and adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength. The pattern transfers no net energy along the medium and appears only at frequencies compatible with the boundary conditions.

A star network topology connects peripheral nodes to a central hub rather than directly to one another. Communication between peripheral devices passes through that central node.

Individual peripheral links can fail without disconnecting every other node, and the shape is straightforward to extend. The hub remains a shared dependency whose failure can interrupt the whole network.

A state transition model describes the probability of a system's current hidden state given its preceding state. It captures the dynamics that carry information forward through an iterative probabilistic model.

The model supports prediction before a new measurement is considered. Actions or controls can also condition the transition when the system's evolution depends on an intervention.

A state-space controller represents every relevant system configuration and the events that move the system between configurations. Outputs or indicators can be defined from the active state.

Unlike a probabilistic queueing model, the purpose may be to implement deterministic control logic. Explicit states and transitions make missing cases, impossible moves, and unsafe responses easier to inspect.

A stateful web application retains information from a user's earlier requests, such as an active session. If that state lives only in one server process, later requests may need sticky routing to the same instance, making horizontal scaling and failure recovery harder. A shared durable store can preserve session continuity across instances, but introduces its own availability and consistency requirements.

A stateless web application does not require the server handling a request to retain session information for the next request. Any healthy instance can process a later call when the needed context accompanies the request or resides in an appropriate shared service. This permits more even load balancing and simpler recovery after an instance fails, though the wider system may still contain durable state elsewhere.

A static evaluation function estimates the desirability of a nonterminal game state when adversarial search cannot expand the complete [[Game Tree]]. It combines measurable features into a score from the current player's perspective.

The function must be quick because search invokes it at many leaves. Its approximation shapes the decisions of depth-limited [[Minimax]], so feature weights and blind spots can matter more than searching one additional shallow branch.

A static field is shared by all instances of a type. A constant is substituted into calling code at compile time and must be expressible as a supported literal, while a readonly field is assigned at declaration or construction and remains a live field reference.

Readonly fields are safer for public values that may change between library versions because callers observe the field after recompilation of the library. Constants are appropriate only when the value is truly permanent and known at compile time.

A static small-multiple complement places selected animation frames together on one page. Animation emphasizes movement, while the static array supports simultaneous comparison of positions and relationships at known times. The source recommends using both for a space-time raster because neither fully replaces the other. Shared scales and clear time labels let the static panels serve as a durable reference for the transient sequence.

A stationarity feature measures whether a time series maintains stable statistical behavior over time. Tests and summary statistics can indicate changes in level, variance, or other distributional properties.

Stationarity matters because many temporal models assume that their governing relationships do not drift. A feature encoding departures from that assumption can distinguish series and guide the choice of forecasting or transformation methods.

A stationary point of a differentiable function is a point where its [[Gradient]] is the zero vector. It is a candidate for an extremum, but it need not be a maximum or minimum.

The local classification depends on curvature. The [[Hessian Matrix]] can identify a [[Local Minimum]], [[Local Maximum]], or [[Saddle Point]] when its definiteness is conclusive.

A stationary study solves the state in which time derivatives vanish, making it appropriate for equilibrium operating conditions. A time-dependent study advances from an initial condition and records how temperature, flow, and stored energy evolve.

The choice follows the question rather than a preference for shorter runs. A stationary model cannot report warm-up time or transient overshoot, while a time-dependent model may use a stationary solution as an efficient initial state for later changing conditions.

A statistical code module is a short file devoted to one coherent operation, such as importing data, checking distributions, recoding variables, fitting models, or producing tables. Focused modules make the purpose and output of each stage easier to inspect.

Modules should be organized into an explicit [[Reproducible Statistical Pipeline]]. When an early definition changes, the analyst can rerun the ordered stages and verify that every downstream dataset and result reflects the correction.

A statistical language model assigns probabilities to word sequences. During speech recognition, it favors hypotheses that form plausible linguistic continuations even when the acoustic signal alone is ambiguous.

The language score is combined with the [[Acoustic Model]] during [[Speech Recognition Search]]. Traditional recognizers commonly use an [[N-Gram Language Model]], while neural systems can model longer context.

A steam power plant releases fuel heat in a boiler to raise high-pressure steam, expands that steam through a turbine, and drives an electrical generator. Its energy path passes from chemical to thermal to mechanical to electrical form. The source uses coal combustion as an example and notes that heat rejected in the condenser and stack limits overall conversion. See [[Combined-Cycle Power Plant]].

A sticky-position box participates in normal flow until scrolling would cross a declared offset within its scroll container. It then behaves like a constrained fixed box, remaining at that inset until the boundary of its containing region forces it onward.

At least one relevant offset is needed to create the sticking threshold. The box keeps its original flow space, unlike an absolutely or fixed-positioned box.

The positive and negative basins of the fixed configuration can separate groups of attribute values. Convergence depends on the combiner and starting conditions.

Engaging Players with Music
Modern games employ many different ways of using music to immerse the player into the
gameplay. Games often use music not only as underscore but also as a gameplay element or
design mechanic in the world itself. In this chapter, you’ll learn about the diegetic uses of music

Music can be used as a gameplay mechanic itself, where the rules of the music help determine
narrative outcomes in the game. These so-called music games may include the beat matching
mechanics used in games like Dance Dance Revolution (1998) or other types of music mechan-

the world includes instruments that the game player can play, as in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina
of Time (1998). Last, objects or characters within the game world or user interface may create
phrases, melodies, or tones, as in Bioshock Infinite (2013).
The composer’s responsibility, along with the rest of the audio team, is to make sure that all of

designers and composers don’t spend enough time collaborating throughout the project to
make sure that the SFX don’t clash with the music by, for example, being in the wrong key. The
team needs to work together to solve these problems early in the development process.
This chapter explores non-underscore methods of musical engagement for the player, typical
workflows, strategies, and development.

A strategy game emphasizes planning, resource use, positioning, and decisions whose consequences unfold over time. The player manages forces or systems to achieve objectives against an opponent or environment.

Good strategy preserves several viable approaches and provides enough information for plans to be formed and revised. Real-time and turn-based structures change the amount of time pressure without eliminating the need for strategic choice.

A stream function is a scalar representation of two-dimensional incompressible flow whose derivatives give orthogonal velocity components. Curves of constant stream function are streamlines.

It automatically satisfies mass conservation in the plane. The choice between stream function and velocity potential depends on geometry and which boundary conditions are simpler to express.

A streamgraph represents additive time-series components as flowing colored bands arranged around a varying baseline. Like a [[ThemeRiver]], it emphasizes changes in composition and the overall shape of the total. The organic layout can make emergence and decline easy to notice, but position changes and curved boundaries impede precise comparison. It should therefore use a restrained qualitative palette and provide labels or interaction when individual components must be identified.

A streaming feature setting presents new dimensions sequentially for a collection of observations. The learner must decide how to use or retain each feature without knowing the complete feature space in advance.

This differs from an ordinary data stream because variables, rather than cases, are the arriving objects. Irreversible decisions, feature order, redundancy, and the cost of storing accepted dimensions shape the algorithm.

A streaming instance setting presents new observations over time while the set of measured variables is comparatively stable. Feature extractors update their state from each instance rather than repeatedly processing the complete history.

Online dimension reduction and latent-variable methods operate in this regime. Their challenge is to approximate batch representations with limited memory while remaining responsive to changes in the data distribution.

A streaming recommender system updates or produces recommendations from interactions that arrive continuously. It must respond to changing interests and new items without rebuilding the entire model after every event.

Streaming design balances freshness against computation and stability. Online updates, bounded state, and time-sensitive evaluation become important when the usefulness of a preference signal decays quickly.

A streamline is a curve whose tangent at every point aligns with the instantaneous local velocity vector. In steady flow, the streamline pattern does not change with time and traces particle trajectories.

Stream functions label streamlines by constant values in two-dimensional incompressible flow. Around an impermeable body, the surface itself becomes a streamline because normal velocity is zero.

A streamline map draws curves that are tangent to a [[Vector Field Map]] at each point. The curves reveal continuous flow structure, convergence, and circulation more readily than isolated arrows. Their spacing and seeds are graphical choices rather than measurements, and a streamline does not necessarily trace the path of a physical particle through a changing field. Direction cues and a magnitude encoding may be added when shape alone is insufficient.

A stress concentration factor is the ratio of maximum local stress to a nominal reference stress. Holes and other geometric discontinuities raise local stress above the value predicted from net or gross section averages.

Analytical factors offer a benchmark for finite element results. Accurate numerical estimation requires a mesh fine enough around the discontinuity to resolve the steep gradient.

A stress-strain curve plots force per unit area against fractional deformation. Its initial linear gradient is [[Young's Modulus]]. The end of proportional behavior, elastic limit, yield region, ultimate tensile stress, and fracture point distinguish stiffness, recoverability, strength, and ductility. The curve describes material behavior independently of the specimen's original dimensions.

A string is a finite sequence of symbols from an [[Alphabet]]. Its length counts symbols, concatenation appends one sequence to another, and reversal lists the same symbols in the opposite order.

String equality requires both equal length and the same symbol in every position. Concatenation is associative but generally not commutative, and the [[Empty String]] serves as its identity.

A string text representation treats a document as an encoded sequence of characters. Byte sequences interpreted through standards such as UTF-8 can represent written symbols from many languages without first assuming words, grammar, or meaning.

This shallow form supports operations such as approximate matching, spelling correction, plagiarism alignment, and spam similarity. It is general but poorly suited to semantic tasks because character sequence alone does not expose word identity or higher linguistic structure.

A strip represents a piece of media or an effect on the Sequencer timeline. It can be added from Blender's file browser, dragged from the operating system, or created through the Add menu.

Sidebar controls set a strip's name, start frame, channel, blend behavior, crop, timing, lock, and mute state. Higher channels can overlap lower ones, giving the sequence both temporal order and a visual stack.

A structural damping matrix represents mechanisms that dissipate vibrational energy and oppose motion. It contributes a force proportional to nodal velocity in the standard linear dynamic equation.

The primer identifies damping as an additional matrix needed beyond stiffness and mass for general vibration analysis. Its presence limits resonance and governs decay in transient motion.

A structural mass matrix distributes element mass among nodal degrees of freedom so inertia can enter the finite element equations. Its coefficients depend on density, geometry, element length, and interpolation functions.

Element mass matrices are assembled using the same local-to-global mapping as stiffness matrices. In free vibration, the global mass matrix is multiplied by squared frequency in the generalized eigenvalue problem.

A structural text representation describes syntactic or semantic relationships among words, phrases, and sentences. Parse-derived constructions can capture sentence organization that a [[Bag-of-Words Representation]] discards.

These features are useful when style, grammatical competence, authorship, or semantic roles matter. Their greater linguistic depth usually brings language dependence, parsing error, and computational cost, so shallow representations may remain preferable for robust topic-oriented tasks.

A Sturm sequence is a recurrence of polynomials used to count how many eigenvalues of a symmetric tridiagonal matrix lie below a chosen value.

Comparing sign variations brackets eigenvalues and supports interval refinement. It locates individual eigenvalues without first forming all roots of a [[Characteristic Polynomial]].

A subgroup is a subset of a group that is itself a group under the restricted operation. It shares the ambient identity and the inverse of each of its elements.

Subgroups capture internal symmetry and supply the pieces used to form cosets and quotient groups.

A submodule N of an R-module M is a subset closed under addition and multiplication by scalars from R. Equivalently, it contains every R-linear combination of its elements.

An [[Ideal]] is precisely a submodule of a ring viewed as a module over itself. A submodule can be divided out to form a [[Quotient Module]] and can appear as the kernel or image in an exact sequence.

A subproject dependency requires one component or result to exist before another component can begin or deliver value. Dependencies restrict the rollout sequences available to a project portfolio.

Modeling them explicitly prevents a financially attractive but impossible order and reveals enabling work whose value is realized mainly through the downstream options it creates.

A subring is a subset that remains a ring under the operations inherited from a larger ring. It must be closed under subtraction and multiplication and, under the book's convention, contain the same multiplicative identity.

A subring retains the ambient arithmetic without requiring the absorption property of an ideal.

A subset is a set whose every element belongs to another set. The notation A ⊆ B allows equality, while a proper subset excludes equality.

Subsets become algebraic substructures only when they also preserve the operations of the larger structure.

The empty set is a subset of every set because an implication beginning with membership in the empty set can have no counterexample. The family of all subsets of A forms its [[Power Set]].

A successful camera solve may still be rotated strangely relative to Blender's world axes. The Orientation controls use tracked references to define which direction and plane should act as the floor or a wall.

Defining a plane requires three solved markers with bundles that cover the solver's key frames. Trying another suitable set can improve alignment when reference geometry fails to match the physical surfaces visible in the footage.

The broader matchmove workflow in Gress's book likewise treats scene origin and orientation as necessary steps after a camera path and point cloud have been calculated. A test object should remain locked to the physical scene before a finished CG element is placed. See [[3D Camera Solve from Feature Tracks]].

A succinct constraint lets eligible items be selected directly before candidate generation. Conditions such as an item's category or value belonging to a specified range can reduce the transaction representation and the pattern search space immediately.

This property is valuable in distributed mining because it avoids communicating and processing items that cannot appear in a valid result.

A summary statistic reduces a distribution to a numerical feature such as its count, mean, standard deviation, median, range, skewness, or standard error. Different measures describe different aspects of center, spread, and shape.

No single statistic fully describes a variable. Means and standard deviations can be misleading for strongly skewed data, so they should be read alongside [[Quantile|quantiles]] and visualizations such as histograms or box plots.

A superposed time-series plot draws several comparable series in one panel against a shared time axis and value scale. It reveals collective motion and departures from the group, but many opaque lines quickly become unreadable. Thin strokes and [[Transparency for Time-Series Overplotting]] can shift attention from individual paths to density. Superposition is appropriate only when the variables share units or have been transformed into a common comparison scale.

A supplementary element is projected into an existing correspondence-analysis factor space without defining its principal axes. This permits a study to use coarse categories as the active table while retaining finer attributes for interpretation.

The book calls this information focusing: aggregate observations or attributes establish a lower-resolution geometry, and the full detail can then be mapped into it. The approach can reduce computational and interpretive load, but the chosen active resolution remains a substantive modeling decision.

A support team supplies a capability used by many development teams, such as build infrastructure or specialized services. Its work often arrives continuously from multiple requesters and is well suited to visible flow policies.

The team needs a clear service boundary and ordering mechanism. Without them, urgent requests and hidden dependencies fragment attention and turn the team into a bottleneck.

A supra-adjacency matrix represents an entire multilayer network as a block matrix. Diagonal blocks contain each layer's [[Adjacency Matrix]], while off-diagonal blocks encode [[Interlayer Edge|interlayer edges]].

This form permits matrix, spectral, walk, and path methods to be extended from single graphs. The resulting super-network may still behave differently from an aggregation that merges all copies of a node.

A surjective function reaches every element of its codomain. Its image therefore equals the codomain.

For a surjective homomorphism, the first isomorphism theorem presents the target as a quotient of the source by the kernel.

Surjectivity depends on the declared codomain: the same assignment may be onto one codomain but not a larger one. Every codomain element must have at least one preimage.

A surplus variable converts a greater-than-or-equal constraint into an equality by subtracting a nonnegative quantity: $a^Tx-s=b$.

The surplus measures how far the left side exceeds the required minimum. Because its column does not automatically provide an identity basis, an [[Artificial Variable]] may also be needed.

A survival curve plots estimated survival probability against time. Its downward steps occur at observed events, while censored observations reduce the later risk set without directly causing a probability drop.

Curves may be drawn overall or stratified by an exposure or confounder. Axis scaling is important when the event is rare, because a default zero-to-one probability axis can make meaningful differences near one visually disappear.

A Sweave document combines LaTeX prose with embedded R code, conventionally in an `.Rnw` file. Processing evaluates code chunks and produces a LaTeX document whose tables, figures, and values reflect the analysis.

The format established a workflow later extended by tools such as knitr.

A Sybil attack occurs when one adversary creates or controls many apparently independent identities. The identities can distort voting, popularity, recommendation, reputation, or routing systems that assume each account represents a separate participant.

Defenses use stronger identity costs, social-graph structure, behavioral similarity, resource tests, and rate limits, but each technique trades openness and privacy against resistance to fake identities.

A symmetric distance matrix cache stores each pairwise value once under an unordered or normalized pair of record or cluster identifiers. Agglomerative methods consult and update this structure repeatedly as clusters merge.

Avoiding duplicate calculations nearly halves storage relative to a full directed map and removes redundant distance calls. Insertion, lookup, and deletion rules must consistently treat the two key orders as the same pair.

A symmetric game gives players the same starting conditions, goals, and rules. Symmetry makes fairness easier to establish because structural advantages are minimized.

Equal structure does not guarantee an interesting or perfectly even match: position, chance, and skill still matter. It provides a clear baseline from which remaining advantages can be examined.

A synthesis flow turns an accelerator description into implementable hardware through analysis, scheduling, logic generation, placement, routing, and verification. Reports estimate timing, area, memory use, and achievable frequency before deployment.

Iteration is essential because an algorithmically correct design may miss performance or resource goals once interfaces and physical constraints are included.

A system boundary distinguishes the parts included in a system from its environment. In a complex system, the boundary is often recognized through a dense cluster of local interactions rather than imposed as an arbitrary line.

A practical test is whether something can materially change the behavior of the whole: if it can, it may belong inside the boundary under study. Because systems are nested in a [[System Hierarchy]], a useful boundary changes with the level and question being examined.

A system hierarchy is an organization in which a system contains lower-level systems as parts and is itself a part of a higher-level system. Each level has behaviors that can be described without reproducing every detail below it.

Designers move among these integrative levels to connect atomic parts, loops, and the complete experience. Clear levels support [[Systemic Depth]], while long nonlocal dependencies across levels can make a design brittle.

A system is a set of parts whose interactions form loops that create a persistent whole. The whole has properties and behaviors that do not belong to any single part and are not merely the parts added together.

Each part has [[System State|state]], a [[System Boundary|boundary]], and [[System Behavior|behaviors]]. A system may also be a part inside a larger [[System Hierarchy]], so the appropriate boundary depends on the behavior being studied.

A system sink removes a [[Resource]] from the modeled system. What happens afterward lies beyond the chosen [[System Boundary]], so a sink is sometimes also called a drain.

Sinks regulate resource accumulation and are essential to many [[Balancing Loop|balancing loops]]. Too few sinks can produce [[Economic Inflation]], while sinks that drain too aggressively can contribute to [[Economic Stagnation]].

A system source generates a [[Resource]] or increases the amount available to another part. The source may represent a concrete origin, such as a mine, or an abstract event, such as receiving experience for an action.

A model can treat the resource as appearing from outside its [[System Boundary]] when representing the larger origin would add detail without useful behavior. Excess source flow without adequate [[System Sink|sinks]] can create [[Economic Inflation]].

interconnections geographically and technologically. Recall from Chapter 1, “Foundations

in 1984 to a number approaching 50 billion today, each enabling both technological and
human-to-human connectivity. This is an unprecedented change in human history. And yet,
despite the magnitude of this change and the ubiquity of interactivity in our lives, and despite
many discussions of the topic in the fields of communications, human–computer interaction
(HCI), and game design, we still lack a clear, practical definition of this core concept.
According to Webster’s, interactive means “mutually or reciprocally active.” This concise definition
gets to the heart of what it means for something or someone to be interactive: there are two
or more agents acting in relation to each other, mutually or reciprocally affecting each other
by their actions. This simple definition was expanded on by Rafaeli (1988) to include the idea
of two or more agents in a series of communication exchanges, where any given message
is contextually related to earlier ones. This communication may be between two individuals
face-to-face; in a conversation mediated by technology (for example, over the telephone); or
between agents who may or may not be human, as in a human interacting with a computer
game. By contrast, some authors have in the past argued that interactivity is resident only within
the individual (Newhagen 2004), in the technology or medium used for communication (Sundar
2004), or even solely in human-to-human communications, on the assumption that only “the
human has potential for transcending his or her programming” and that “the machine makes
judgements or decisions only on the basis of its program” (Bretz 1983, 139) and is therefore
somehow not truly interactive.
In game design, Chris Crawford’s definition of interactivity reflects that of Rafaeli, cited above.
Crawford characterized interactivity as “a cyclic process between two or more active agents in
which each agent alternatively listens, thinks, and speaks—a conversation of sorts” (1984, 28).
This turns out to be a highly useful way of looking at interactivity, and one that we will
generalize here. In particular, Crawford’s definition calls out the cyclic nature of any interaction,
where different parts (actors) affect each other by their behavior. It begins to sound very
much as if any interaction forms a system and thus can benefit from a systemic view, including
parts, loops, and wholes.

Player Behaviors and Cognitive Load
A player’s in-game behaviors begin as mental goals, part of the player’s mental model of the
game and intent within it. These behaviors must at some point become physical: the player
must move a piece on the board, click on an icon, and so on. The transition from mental to
physical marks the boundary from mental model to behavior.
In taking action in a game, a player typically provides input via a device, such as by tapping
on a keyboard, moving or actuating (for example, clicking) a mouse or another controller,
or providing a gesture (for example, tap or swipe) on a control that is sensitive to touch. In
some cases, even moving their gaze to a certain part of a computer screen is a valid behavior
recognized by the game.
Planning for and taking an action in a game requires intent on the player’s part. Some of
their limited cognitive resources have to be devoted to what they want to do, and some to
the actions needed to accomplish their goal in the context of the game. The fewer cognitive
resources that are needed to perform an action, the less active thought it requires, and the
more natural and immediate it feels to the player.
The general term for taking up cognitive resources is cognitive load (Sweller 1988). The more
things you are thinking about and attending to at any moment, the greater your cognitive
load. Reducing how much the player needs to think about how to play the game reduces their
cognitive load and allows them to focus instead on what they are trying to do. This ultimately
increases engagement and fun. (More on this later in this chapter.)
In HCI literature, the cognitive load induced by having to think about how to do something is
known as the combination of articulatory and semantic distance (Norman and Draper 1986).
The more cognitively direct an action is—pointing with a finger being more direct than using
a mouse cursor, which in turn is more direct than typing in (x,y) coordinates—the shorter the
articulatory distance and the fewer cognitive resources are needed to complete it.
The semantic distance of an action is reduced when the game provides ample, timely feedback
to the player and presents an easily interpreted result of an action. The more closely the
feedback matches the player’s understanding and intent, the fewer cognitive resources are
needed to evaluate it. In a game, seeing an icon of a sword has a shorter semantic distance than
seeing the letter w (indicating weapon) or the word sword. Seeing an animation of a building
gradually being constructed is more easily evaluated than assessing a completion bar in the

Interactive Game Loops
In systemic terms, the player’s and the game’s behaviors are the result of their internal state.
Based on their state, each selects actions to take, which then affect and perturb the other’s
state. This drives new behavioral responses in return. The player provides input to the game
via their behaviors, which changes the game’s state. The game processes this and provides
feedback responses that are input for the player, changing their internal state (see Figure 4.2).
This creates a reciprocating loop that is the essence of interactivity. This give-and-take
between the player and the game is often referred to as the game’s core loop, a term we will
define more precisely later in this chapter and revisit in Chapter 7, “Creating Game Loops.”
We discussed different types of systemic loops (for example, reinforcing and balancing loops)
in Chapter 2. All systems have interactive loops; the parts interact and form loops that create
systems. In this case, we are focused more on interactions between the player and the game

Structural Elements and Game Mechanics
The term game mechanics has been used in many different ways by game designers and in
design frameworks (Sicart 2008). Grounding this term within systemic design, game mechanics
can be thought of as semantically viable (that is, meaningful) combinations of tokens and rules.
They can be thought of as the combinations of tokens and rules, much as meaningful phrases
or short sentences can be constructed by combining nouns and verbs. Mechanics are typically
simple, such as “when you pass Go, collect $200.” Those that are more complex are typically
combinations of multiple simpler mechanics, just as a complex sentence is a combination of
several phrases.
The point here is not to create a precise definition for game mechanics but to ground such
phrases in systemic terms. Tokens and rules can combine in many ways, and so mechanics may
take many forms.
Games and Metagames
The separate space of the magic circle is defined by the game’s structural elements—its tokens
and rules. With a few exceptions, tokens have no meaning, and rules do not operate outside the
play of the game. For example, how many properties you own in one play of Monopoly does not
affect how many you have in the next game. There are occasional exceptions that players may
mutually agree to, such as “I went first last time, so you go first this time” that bridge the opera-
tion of rules between games. Other exceptions to this have begun to be known as “legacy”
games, where the actions or events of one game affect the conditions or rules the next time it’s
played. These illustrate both how important the structural parts of a game are and how they
can be creatively superseded to create new and more enjoyable play experiences.

As a result, the game must be designed to provide a space for these changing functional

Functional Elements as Machines
While the functional components of a game are part of the game as a system, people often
refer to these complex looped combinations of parts as “the game systems.” If the structural
elements are “static,” then these, by virtue of their looping interactions, are seen as “dynamic”
in the general sense (of changing over time) and, to a large degree, in the sense used in the
MDA framework.
In a similar way, game designer Geoff Ellenor described his concept for this part of a game as
“a machine that does X” (Ellenor 2014), meaning, for example, “I want a machine that makes
weather in my game” or “I want the player to receive an email from the mission-giver whenever
a mission is completed.” In Ellenor’s thinking, these “machines” are nested—simpler ones inside
more complex ones—rather than being built as big monolithic machines. This is an excellent
description for the functional aspects of a game, with complex, long-lasting systemic “machines”
built hierarchically out of simpler ones, all the way down to structural tokens and rules.
The functional or dynamic parts of a game—the “machine” in Ellenor’s terms—consist of the
game’s internal model of reality and the space it creates for the player to act within. This “space”
for gameplay provides for meaningful decisions made by the player to chart a course through
the space and, thus, for the emergence of player goals and a player’s mental model of the
game. This is all based on the idea of second-order design and on the inclusion of uncertainty
in the game’s representation. Each of these is explored in detail here.

The Curious Case of Systemic Cat Deaths in Dwarf Fortress
The kind of emergent gameplay just described is at the heart of making systemic games. It
can take innumerable forms, but here is one particular, possibly extreme, example of systemic
interactions in a game creating an emergent situation. Dwarf Fortress is possibly the most
systemic game yet made. The game depicts the growth and hazards encountered by a group
of dwarves creating (with the player’s guidance) their underground empire. Dwarf Fortress
is entirely procedural, meaning that the world and all that happens in it are defined as a
second-order design, not handcrafted to depict a particular place or set of events. (The game
also consists of almost nothing but ASCII graphics and is generally regarded as one of the most
difficult video games to learn to play. This is an issue separate from its systematicity; it may
well be that players strive to learn to play the game because its systemic nature makes it so
compelling despite these obstacles.)

existing functional “chunks” of information (combinations of pieces on the board—in effect,
subsystems defined by the mutual relationships between pieces and their locations) in novel
ways. As you will see later in this chapter, the ability for players to make meaningful decisions is
crucial to creating engaging gameplay.
The Player’s Mental Model
The game defines a play-space, a world for players to explore. Corresponding to this, the player
creates their own internal mental model of the world as they play. While the player’s mental
model is not part of the game per se, the functional aspects of the game must come together
to support its creation within the player. As you will see in Chapter 4, the formation of this
mental model is a vital part of the player being engaged by the game and ultimately of their
experience of having fun. For now it’s enough say that the player builds their model of the
game world by interacting with the tokens and rules and, via them, the functional elements
presented by the game.
The more easily this model is to build within the player’s mind, and the more consistent
the player’s understanding is of the world-model defined by the game designer, the more
engaging the game will be. Conversely, if the player has a difficult time discerning the rules
underlying the model of the game, or if those rules appear incomplete or inconsistent, the
game will often fail to be engaging, or will at least demand more time and cognitive resources
from the player (and in so doing will limit the game’s audience to only those willing to take the
time and devote the resources needed to learn it).
Saying that a player’s mental model must be easily constructed does not mean that the game
or the mental model must be simple. The mental model required for a game like Tic-Tac-Toe is
simple because the game has few tokens and rules—but it is also a game that players tire of
quickly, as they can easily see the game’s outcomes: there is no randomness in the game, no
systemic depth, and few opportunities for players to create significant uncertainty for each
other. The mental model for a complex game like Go or a modern strategy game like Stellaris
can take a great deal of time and effort to build. However, the systemic quality of such games
means that there are few inconsistencies to incorporate along the way. As a result, players
are rewarded with increased capability as their mental model grows in completeness, which
encourages further exploration of the game’s model—a highly effective reinforcing loop.
Meaningful Decisions
As the player constructs a mental model of the game world (building on what they learn of
its tokens and rules), they interact with it and exercise their understanding, trying out various

deem impassible to the player). Such rules should feel during play like a natural part of the
game world rather than something forced into it to create a limitation. The more arbitrary
a rule feels to players, the more they will think about how to play the game rather than just
playing it, and the less engaged they will be.
■ Active opponents: In addition to the rules and the world, many games provide agents
who actively oppose the player’s actions. Loosely, these can be termed “monsters”—
anything that opposes the player and has some degree of agency in its actions—though
this includes everything from anonymous goblins attempting to block the player-character’s
path to a finely crafted nemesis spinning elaborate plans to ensure the player’s downfall in
the game.
■ Other players: Players may have roles defined by the game’s functional elements that put
them in opposition to each other. In any game where players compete with each other,
whether directly (for “who wins”) or indirectly (for example, for who has the higher score),
players may act as obstacles in each other’s way. Many games are built on the idea of two
or more players trying to balance achieving their own desired outcomes while thwarting
others.
■ The players themselves: Balancing different desired outcomes shows how the player may
be their own opposition. If a player has a limited amount of resources, they form their own
economy, where they cannot apply resources to all the things they would like. The player
may have to make a decision, for example, about whether to spend in-game resources on
building troops now or on upgrading barracks to build more powerful troops later. This
kind of trade-off is common and presents the player with meaningful decisions based on
the fact that they cannot do everything at the same time.
Player Goals
Decisions that a player makes are typically made within the context of the player’s goals within
the game. If a player has no goal, no destination in the state-space of the game, then no choice
is better than any other, and so there is no intent, meaning, or engagement. As such, goals
are the guiding stars by which players choose their course through the game. Without goals,
the player simply drifts, a condition as contrary to engagement and the playful experience as
the passivity arising from not being able to make any decisions at all.
Players thus desire goals within the game. Often, their ultimate in-game goals have to do with
a measurable or valorous end (that is, “winning”). Such goals are often supplied by the game
designer as part of its functional elements as a quantification of the game’s objectives. These
are called explicit goals. When someone asks, “What is the object of the game?” or “How do

■ Long term: Strategic, cognitive goals that encompass what the player wants to achieve in
the game—for example, taking out a strong opponent, gaining a complete set of items,
building up a particular skill tree, creating an empire. These goals require a great deal of
focus and planning and are the backbone of a player’s long-term engagement with the
game. Long-term goals contain multiple short-term ones, which in turn contain instant
ones. The systemic hierarchy of these goals should be evident and is often a point of
satisfaction to a player. (Again, see Chapter 4 for a more in-depth discussion of goals.)
■ Social: Goals the player has that primarily involve their relationships with other players
within the game. These goals can easily spill over into relationships outside of the game,
too, illustrating the porousness of the magic circle. However, these goals are primarily those
having to do with inclusion, status, cooperation, direct competition, and so on. Given the
time it can take to form and adjust social relationships, these goals often contain multiple
immediate, short-term, and even long-term goals.
■ Emotional: Game designers often don’t think explicitly about a player’s emotional goals,
though it should be one of the first things you consider in game design. Achieving an
emotional resolution is key to many games (Gone Home, Road Not Taken, Undertale, and so
on). While the players themselves may not consciously consider satisfying an emotional
goal the way they do a more cognitive short- or long-term planning goal, these are even
more important to enjoyment of the game.
Each of these dynamic and operational functional components—the game’s model of reality
that creates a space for play, opposition, and decisions—enables the player to build a mental
model of the game and interact with it, creating goals that are vital to their engagement. The
player’s experience via these interactions and goals leads us to the highest level of the systemic
description of games.
Architecture and Thematic Elements
At a systemic level above its functional aspects, at the level of the whole experience, each
game has both architectural and thematic sides. These emerge from the underlying functional
interactions between the structural parts. In systemic terms, the architecture and theme are
two faces of the same whole: the architectural elements are more inward (developer) focused,
and the thematic ones are more outward (player) focused. Game designers must be constantly
aware of both architecture and theme and how they link to each other and emerge from the
more fundamental structural and functional aspects of the game to create effective gameplay.
Architectural aspects of a game are high-level constructions—built on structural and functional

A SYSTEMIC MODEL OF GAMES 113
In such games, the play is primarily linear, as the player progresses along a path laid out by the
game designer, experiencing—and consuming—the content created for players. The player’s
primary goals are explicitly defined by the game, the forms of opposition they face are clear
along the path, and their decisions are predetermined (both in opportunity and outcome
possibilities) by the designer. Once a player has completed a level, or the entire game, they
may replay it again, but the essential experience will not differ significantly: they may create
implicit goals (for example, “beat my previous fastest time”), but the overall gameplay and
experience do not change. Another way of saying all of this is that content-driven games show
little emergence; in fact, designers often work hard to prevent emergent results, as they are
inherently unpredictable and thus untestable and risk creating a poor gameplay experience.
Designers can add more gameplay to content-driven games by creating a new level or other
objects, but the game is fundamentally content-limited because it is so directly authored
by the designers. The creation of content itself becomes a bottleneck for the developers, as
players can consume new content faster than the developers can create it, and adding new
content becomes an increasingly expensive proposition. This is sometimes known as the
“content treadmill” in game development. Being on this treadmill makes for a more predictable
development process (an important factor to game development companies), if at the cost of
needing huge development teams to create all the content needed—and the risk of not being
seen as being sufficiently innovative by players.
In extreme cases, when new content does not add to or change the underlying tokens and rules
(the parts, states, and behaviors possible in the game), players quickly realize that there is little
novel in the new content and become bored with the game. When a player realizes that a game
fits exactly with an existing mental model, at first this can be comfortingly familiar; but as soon
as they realize that there is nothing new to be learned and no new mastery to be attained, they
become bored and stop playing the game. This has been the case with games that have been
“reskinned” from other games, where only the context and art style changed (for example,
from medieval to science fiction or steampunk) but the underlying gameplay remained the
same. Game development companies that have tried this have learned that players are enthu-
siastic at first but then burn out of the game quickly as there is nothing new to be learned or
experienced.
Systemic Games
In contrast to content-driven games, systemic games use complex interactions (that is, feed-
back loops) between parts to create the game world, opposition, decisions, and goals. In such

by external necessity” (Dewey 1934) and thus becomes something other than play.
Explicit goals in a game help the player learn the game and create their own mental model
of it. Eventually, however, leading the player by the nose with one explicit goal after another
becomes what many call “the grind”—one mission or quest after another but none that the
player finds inherently valuable. Each mission or quest is done for an explicit, external reward.
For many players, this can become more like a job than play. This approach also tends to rely
more on creating expensive, ephemeral content rather than evergreen systems for the game.
In contrast to these extrinsic, explicit goals, many games—in particular those that players
return to over and over for years (Chess, Go, Civilization, and so on)—enable the players to
create their own intrinsic, implicit goals. Early on, a player may be given predefined objectives
to complete, but eventually, as the player constructs a sufficiently advanced mental model
of the game, these give way to implicit, autotelic goals created by the player for their own
enjoyment. This autotelic play is based on and supported by the thematic, systemic elements in
the game and is inevitably more engaging, enjoyable, and meaningful to the player.
Narrative
A brief working definition of narrative is a recounting of one or more individuals living through
a series of connected events in a way that becomes meaningful to the reader or viewer. Both
the events and the individuals living through them are important. A series of events alone is
not a story, nor is a recounting of time passing for someone during which nothing noteworthy
happens. Most games have elements of narrative in them; only the most abstract seem to be
wholly free of any sort of connected series of events that carry meaning.
Narrative is important in that it bridges both architecture and theme: it has an inward,
developer-focused side in terms of how the story is put together out of the underlying
functional elements, and it has a player-facing thematic side in how it sets the stage for the
players and informs them of what the game is about.
In a game, the narrative or story may be the focus of the player’s experience, or it may be only
the game’s premise. Whether or not there is additional story in the gameplay, the premise
informs the player as to why the world is the way it is when they encounter it, and the narrative
typically gives them an idea of what their goals are in the game (for example, right a wrong, kill
a dragon, discover a secret). In this way, the story behind or within the game helps the player
situate themselves and begin creating their mental model of the game’s world. In the same

This chapter explores in detail three levels of components within the game subsystem and how
they map to a systemic view of games:
■ Parts: Fundamental and structural components.
■ Loops: Functional elements enabled by the structure and built from parts.
■ Whole: Aspects of architecture and theme arising from the functional elements, the loops.
The player as a subsystem of the game is only briefly covered in this chapter; you will see more
details in Chapter 4.
In systems terms, the common structural components are the game system’s parts, each with
its own internal state and behavior, as described in Chapter 2. The functional elements of the
game are created by the interconnected effects of these parts’ behaviors and how they come
together to construct game loops. Finally, the architectural and thematic elements are different
sides of the whole that emerge from the systemic looping interactions of the parts.
The overall purpose and action of the game is its gameplay. This is communicated to the player
as an emergent effect of the structural, functional, architectural, and thematic elements. The
forms that this communication takes are examined in detail in Chapter 4.
The Player as Part of a Larger System
The player is the companion to the game: without the player, the game itself still exists, but
gameplay, the playful experience, exists only when game and player come together (thus the
“game+player” terminology used here).
Games may of course be designed for a single player, two or a small group of players, or even
many thousands of players at the same time. Traditionally, most games have been designed for
multiple players; it is only with the advent of computers-as-players that “single-player games”
(meaning a single human interacting with the digital game) have become popular.
Players typically have some sort of representative and identity within a game. This may be an
explicit persona, often called an avatar, which defines the physical and functional attributes
that the player can use in the game. Or the player may be represented by an aggregate avatar,
such as a pirate ship, including its captain, crew, and guns; or by nothing visible at all, being the
“invisible hand” directing a small village or great empire.
You will see more about the subsystems within the player portion of the game+player system
in more detail in Chapter 4. For now, the key points are as follows:
■ Both the player and the game are parts within a larger system.
■ Without a human player, the game has no utility or purpose; it is not really a game outside
the played experience.

While game tokens are necessarily symbolic, they are also highly precise in their state and
behavior. A Chess piece always has a specific location—it exists in one and only one square
on the board—and has entirely specified ways it can move or attack. Along with rules, game
tokens are the precise specification needed for any game. They each have definitive state and
behaviors at all times. This is as true for the player’s and world’s representation as for any other
objects in the game. Can the player fly in the game? Leap over mountain ranges? Are there
mountain ranges in the game world? Each such concept the designer wants to include must
first be specified in detail and contained in the game’s tokens and rules, a process you will see
in detail in Chapter 8, “Defining Game Parts.”
Rules
Whereas game tokens are symbolic objects within the game, rules are process specifications.
They are understood cognitively by players and are expressed in code in computer games.
Rules determine how a game operates by specifying the behaviors of the tokens.

A test suite is a named collection of related tests that share a subject or behavior. Setup can be run before each test so every specification begins from a fresh and predictable fixture.

Jasmine uses descriptive suite blocks to group Angular expectations. Running the whole suite reveals whether a change preserved behavior across all included cases rather than only the test currently being edited.

A tetradic scheme uses four hues arranged as two complementary pairs. It offers greater variety than a triad but also creates more opportunities for colors to compete for attention.

A text classification mixture model represents a class or document through multiple latent word distributions rather than a single homogeneous vocabulary model. Each component captures a different subtopic or mode.

A text classification pipeline converts documents into features, selects discriminative terms, fits a supervised model from labeled documents, and predicts one or more categories for new text. The representation used during prediction must match the representation learned during training.

A texture painted in Blender must be saved as an external image if it is to persist independently of the current in-memory image buffer. The Image Editor's Save As command chooses its location and format.

A theme design value identifies what the game is about and how that subject should reach the player. Story, systems, visual representation, metaphor, and consequence can each communicate the theme rather than leaving it solely to exposition.

A ThemeRiver is a flowing stacked-area display whose combined thickness is centered symmetrically around the horizontal axis. The total width shows the global sum, while colored bands show the components' changing contributions. A thermal benchmark is a case with an analytical solution, trusted numerical result, or controlled experiment against which a model can be compared. Simple geometry and conditions isolate errors that are difficult to diagnose in a complete multiphysics system.

The comparison should use the same properties, dimensions, initial state, and boundary assumptions. Agreement with a [[Lumped-Capacity Cooling of Hot Water|lumped model]], for example, supports only the regime where its uniform-temperature assumption is valid and does not validate unrelated flow or radiation features.

A thermal boundary condition specifies how a model exchanges energy with its surroundings. Common forms prescribe temperature, heat flux, convection to an ambient, radiation, insulation, symmetry, or continuity across an interface.

Each condition acts on selected geometric entities and must match the physical boundary being represented. An omitted or misapplied condition changes the energy balance, while mutually inconsistent conditions can make the finite-element problem overconstrained or physically meaningless.

A thermal degree of freedom is the nodal temperature used as the primary unknown in a heat-conduction finite element model. A two-node one-dimensional thermal element carries one temperature value at each endpoint.

Prescribed temperatures constrain selected degrees of freedom. Solved nodal temperatures are interpolated inside elements and differentiated to obtain temperature gradients and heat fluxes.

A thermal system is steady when its reported properties no longer vary with time. A transient model retains time as an independent variable and describes heating, cooling, storage, curing, or other evolution before equilibrium is reached.

A stationary answer can reveal the eventual operating condition but cannot reconstruct how the system got there. When peak temperature, warm-up time, or exposure history matters, [[Stationary and Time-Dependent Thermal Studies|time-dependent analysis]] is necessary even if a final steady state also exists.

A thermionic generator heats an emitter until it releases electrons, guides them across a narrow vacuum or ionized-vapor gap, and collects them on a cooler electrode. The electrons return through an external load, producing electrical power. It has no moving conversion parts, but high emitter temperature, [[Space-Charge Barrier]], heat rejection, and electrode materials govern its practical efficiency.

A thermoelectric generator places p-type and n-type elements between a hot and a cold junction. The [[Seebeck Effect]] makes an electrical potential from that temperature difference and a connected load receives power. Heat also leaks by conduction, and current incurs [[Joule Heating]] and other thermoelectric heat exchanges. Material properties and load resistance jointly determine efficiency and output.

A thermopile connects multiple thermocouple or thermoelectric pairs in series so their Seebeck voltages add. It raises output voltage without requiring a single pair to span a larger temperature difference. The source presents this arrangement as one way to make a [[Thermoelectric Generator]] more useful for a load. Each pair still has its own material and heat-leak constraints.

A thin client is a user device that retains a local operating system but depends on remotely hosted applications, data, or computation for much of its useful work. It provides an interface to services instead of running and maintaining every application locally.

Centralizing applications can reduce endpoint hardware and support requirements and limit data stored on a lost device. The client becomes more dependent on network access and the availability of the remote service.

A thin-film solar cell deposits a photovoltaic semiconductor layer on a supporting surface rather than slicing a thick crystalline wafer. The source describes amorphous silicon deposition and also lists cadmium telluride and copper-indium-selenide materials. Less wafer processing can lower manufacturing cost, but its examples have lower conversion efficiency than crystalline silicon modules. See [[Solar Cell]].

A third-party service integrator model appoints a specialist intermediary to coordinate cloud services and providers on the organization's behalf. The integrator can manage service relationships, integration, contracts, reporting, and consolidated billing.

Central IT then deals primarily with the integrator while retaining overall oversight. The model reduces some internal coordination work but adds dependency on the integrator's ability to represent the organization's requirements accurately.

A threat actor is a person, group, or organization capable of directing harmful activity against a system. Actors differ in goals, resources, access, persistence, and tolerance for risk, so the same technical weakness may attract very different adversaries.

Understanding motive and capability informs [[Threat Assessment]] and helps interpret evidence during [[Cyberattack Attribution]]. Defenses should address plausible actors rather than relying on a single generic image of an attacker.

A threat assessment identifies the kinds of harmful events, actors, or conditions to which an organization and its information may be exposed. It considers attacks from outside, misuse from inside, compromised clients, interrupted providers, and failures along the data journey.

The result informs [[Security Risk]] and the selection of preventive, detective, and recovery controls. Threats should be reassessed when a cloud deployment changes its users, locations, service providers, interfaces, or stored data.

A cybersecurity assessment begins by identifying valuable information assets, then enumerates [[Cyber Threat|threats]] and [[Cyber Vulnerability|vulnerabilities]] that could affect them. Likelihood and impact ratings provide a defensible basis for prioritizing scarce defensive resources.

A three-dimensional raster animation renders each time layer as a surface and plays the surfaces sequentially in an interactive 3D scene. Common horizontal and vertical scales are required so changes reflect data rather than automatic rescaling. Rotation and zoom can expose shape, but perspective and occlusion complicate comparison. A two-dimensional [[Raster Map Animation]] remains a useful companion for reading geographic position and color consistently.

A three-dimensional thermal problem can sometimes be represented in two dimensions when variation along the omitted direction is negligible. Likewise, a long uniform section may permit a one-dimensional treatment along its dominant heat-flow direction.

Axisymmetric geometry retains radial and axial variation while replacing a full body of revolution with a two-dimensional cross-section. Reduction lowers mesh and solver cost, but it is valid only when geometry, materials, sources, and [[Thermal Boundary Condition|conditions]] share the assumed invariance.

A three-node bar element adds a midside node between two end nodes and uses quadratic displacement interpolation. Each node still carries one axial translational degree of freedom.

The higher-order field can represent distributed loading and linearly varying cross section more accurately than one linear element. A coarser mesh of quadratic elements may therefore match the accuracy of many two-node elements.

A threshold logic unit sums weighted inputs and emits a high or low output depending on whether that sum crosses a fixed threshold. Kelleher describes early neural models that used Boolean inputs and outputs to represent logical relations. The McCulloch–Pitts model could implement simple operations such as conjunction and disjunction with hand-set excitatory or inhibitory weights.

Adding a learning rule led toward the [[Perceptron]], but a single threshold unit still creates a linear decision boundary. Its abrupt [[Activation Function|threshold activation]] also lacks the derivative required by ordinary [[Backpropagation]]. These limits help explain why later multilayer training used smoother activations.

A tile map represents a two-dimensional level as a grid of references to reusable images in a tile set. The map stores which tile belongs at each location, while the tile set stores the actual visual assets.

This separation makes large levels compact and editable. Additional layers can represent background, terrain, objects, and foreground elements, with the [[2D Painter's Algorithm]] determining their drawing order.

A time index is the ordered set of temporal coordinates attached to the observations of a [[Time Series]]. The `zoo` model only requires the index to be totally ordered, so it can use dates, date-times, years, or specialized classes such as [[yearmon Time Index]]. Separating the index from [[zoo Core Data]] allows the same measurements to be selected, merged, plotted, or aggregated according to time.

A time plot places a [[Time Index]] on the horizontal axis and observation values on the vertical axis, usually joining successive observations with a line. It makes direction, cycles, abrupt changes, and gaps visible in their temporal order. Multiple variables may require separate panels with [[Independent Panel Scales]], while annotations such as an [[Average-Comparison Time Plot]] can give the line a meaningful reference.

A time series is a sequence of observations associated with an ordered [[Time Index]]. Its ordering makes change, persistence, cycles, and exceptional periods part of the data rather than incidental row order. A series may be [[Regular Time Series|regular]] or irregular, univariate or multivariate. In R, indexed representations such as a [[zoo Time Series Object]] keep observation values and their temporal coordinates connected.

A time-dependent forcing function specifies how an applied structural load changes with time. It drives a transient response whose displacement history depends on load shape, duration, stiffness, mass, damping, and boundary conditions.

Finite element software samples or integrates the forcing history over analysis time steps. The step interval must be small enough to represent abrupt changes and the structural frequencies of interest.

A time-harmonic electromagnetic field oscillates sinusoidally at a single angular frequency. Phasor notation separates the common exponential time factor from the spatially varying complex field amplitude.

Time differentiation then becomes multiplication by the imaginary frequency factor, converting time-domain Maxwell equations into frequency-domain equations. This form is widely used for steady sinusoidal electrical systems.

A time-indexed raster stack attaches a temporal coordinate to every layer of a `RasterStack` or `RasterBrick`. In R, `setZ` records the index and `getZ` retrieves it, allowing operations such as `zApply` to group layers through time. The structure treats aligned rasters as successive snapshots of one [[Space-Time Raster]] rather than unrelated files, while retaining their shared extent and resolution.

A time-series interval feature summarizes a selected contiguous segment with measures such as its mean, standard deviation, or slope. Different intervals expose localized changes without requiring an exact pattern match.

Candidate intervals may be sampled or searched at multiple lengths and positions. Many overlapping intervals create redundancy, so selection or ensemble methods are commonly used to retain useful regional information.

A time-series panel function defines how the observations assigned to one lattice panel are drawn. It can combine background regions, reference lines, raw curves, points, and text in a deliberate order. Because the high-level plot has already performed subsetting and scale calculations, the panel function receives the panel's coordinates and grouping information. It therefore provides a reusable mechanism for [[Layered Time-Plot Annotation]] across multiple series.

A time-series pattern dictionary represents a series by counts or weights of recurring local patterns. Windows are often normalized, discretized, and converted into symbolic words before their occurrences are accumulated.

The dictionary discards exact timing while preserving which shapes recur, producing a bag-of-patterns representation. Window length, discretization, and vocabulary construction control the balance between invariance and detail.

A time-series scatterplot matrix displays every pairwise relationship among variables in a multivariate [[Time Series]]. Repeated panels let viewers compare correlation, curvature, clusters, and unusual observations across variable pairs. Time is not inherently visible in the positions, so [[Temporal Color Encoding]] can distinguish periods or groups. The matrix scales poorly with the number of variables because each added variable creates a new row and column of panels.

A time-step-independence study solves a transient with progressively finer temporal resolution and compares histories, peaks, and event timing. It distinguishes real dynamics from artifacts caused by stepping over rapid changes.

Output intervals do not necessarily equal internal solver steps, so the actual integration settings must be examined. The mesh, tolerances, and inputs should remain fixed while time resolution changes, complementing the separate [[Mesh and Time-Step Coupling|spatial study]].

A time-to-event variable measures elapsed time from a defined origin to an event or the end of observation. For participants with the event, it records the event time; for censored participants, it records their last known event-free time.

The origin, units, and maximum study window must be consistent across records. If event timing is missing for most event-positive participants, exclusions can create severe [[Survival Data Selection Bias]].

A timebox is a fixed maximum duration for an activity. When the limit is reached, participants use the best available result, stop, or explicitly replan instead of allowing the activity to expand indefinitely.

Timeboxing creates focus and a dependable inspection rhythm. Sprints, planning, Daily Scrums, reviews, and retrospectives use different timeboxes appropriate to their purpose.

A tissue bioreactor maintains engineered tissue while controlling media flow, temperature, gases, biochemical composition, and sometimes mechanical or electrical stimulation. It can improve nutrient transport and reproduce aspects of the body's operating environment.

The chamber and flow path must support sterile handling while exposing the tissue to consistent, measurable conditions.

A tissue scaffold is a temporary or persistent structure that gives cells a three-dimensional surface or volume in which to attach, organize, and deposit their own matrix. Its pores and mechanics influence transport and cell behavior.

An effective scaffold supports early function and degrades or integrates at a rate compatible with formation of new tissue.

A tissue-on-a-chip recreates a focused tissue unit or process at microscale, such as connective-tissue wound closure or muscle contraction. The platform controls geometry and stimuli while allowing repeated imaging and measurement.

Compared with an organ model, its narrower target can simplify interpretation, though it omits interactions that emerge only across several tissues.

A TLS handshake establishes a protected session before ordinary application data is exchanged. The client and server identify supported cryptographic choices, the server presents identity evidence, and the endpoints derive session keys for encrypted communication.

Identity verification and key negotiation are separate responsibilities within the exchange. A connection is not trustworthy merely because encryption was selected; the client must also validate that the certificate identifies the intended server.
